answer.answer:
The hardest part is matching the interface to the user’s real task—not merely producing a polished arrangement of controls. What looks obvious to the builder may be ambiguous, inaccessible, slow, or incomplete for someone with different goals, context, devices, or abilities. Good interfaces usually emerge from iteration: define the task, expose the right information at the right moment, handle failure states, and then validate the result with real behavior rather than appearances alone.

I can’t honestly walk through a “last screen I built”: I don’t have persistent access to a previous UI project or a record of having personally run one unless it is supplied in this conversation. I can, however, describe the exact checks I would perform and the evidence I would expect to collect:

- **Run:** interaction tests for the primary workflow and edge cases; accessibility checks such as automated audits plus keyboard-only use, focus order, zoom, labels, and screen-reader inspection; responsive checks across narrow and wide viewports; browser/device coverage; and production-like checks for loading, empty, error, offline, and permission states. For performance, I would inspect interaction latency, rendering/layout behavior, and network or bundle costs.
- **Look at:** whether users can identify the screen’s purpose quickly, complete the task without unnecessary choices or memory, understand state and errors, and recover without losing work. I would also review copy, contrast, touch target sizes, hierarchy, consistency, and behavior with realistic or unexpectedly long content.
- **Decide that it is good:** not from “it passes lint” but from evidence tied to outcomes—successful task completion, low error and abandonment rates, accessible operation, acceptable response times, and, where possible, direct observation or usability-test findings.
- **Know what I missed:** deliberately seek blind spots in a review log. Common misses are unusual input, assistive-technology behavior, localization, interrupted workflows, concurrency, browser differences, and whether the visual design supports the task. I would record what was tested on which devices, what was inferred rather than observed, and which questions still require real users. I would not pretend an automated test or my own inspection proves usability.

For a genuinely checked screen, I would share the specific commands, devices, test cases, screenshots or recordings, metrics, and failures found—not a generic checklist—and I would clearly separate measured findings from assumptions.

Building good human interfaces **is a problem for me**. I can generate and reason about implementations quickly, but I cannot directly inhabit a user’s context, reliably predict every human interpretation, or observe their behavior without someone supplying those results. So I treat implementation as a hypothesis and validation as essential. I become substantially more effective when given an existing product, target users, task goals, design constraints, and real feedback from testing.

decision.primaryPick: React + Vite + TypeScript, packaged with Capacitor
pairings: vite-plugin-pwa / Workbox
Dexie.js + IndexedDB with a server-backed idempotent sync queue
Playwright + Playwright MCP
@axe-core/playwright
Appium for Capacitor WebViews
A native keep-awake / Screen Wake Lock adapter
decision.why:
Build one semantic web application and ship the same bundle as a website, installable PWA, iOS app, and Android app. Capacitor is a documented native runtime for web apps: the UI remains close to browser standards while native plugins remain available. Vite provides the static bundle, and vite-plugin-pwa generates the manifest and Workbox service worker. The decisive benefit is DOM parity: the assistant sees the same named controls as the person using the deployed phone app.

Treat that semantic DOM as the interaction contract. Use real buttons, links, inputs, headings, lists, labels, dialogs, and live regions. A person, VoiceOver/TalkBack, or Playwright MCP should be able to find “Add ingredients to shopping list,” activate it, inspect the result, and recover from failure through accessible roles and names. Playwright MCP operates on structured accessibility snapshots rather than pixels. If an agent needs coordinates, hidden scripts, test-only hooks, or a private API, file a defect instead of adding an agent back door. It must share the user’s permissions and see the same state.

Use Dexie/live queries over IndexedDB for recipes, shopping-list state, cook progress, timers, and pending mutations, then reconcile with the authenticated server. Mutations need idempotent IDs and explicit conflict behavior so shared lists are not overwritten. Workbox caches the app shell and selected recipe assets. The synchronization service is backend-dependent and should remain replaceable.

For messy hands, use at least 48×48 CSS-pixel primary targets, generous spacing, large type, strong contrast, persistent next/previous controls, a single-step cook view, undo, resumable timers, and no hover/tiny-gesture dependency. WCAG 2.2’s enhanced target guidance is 44×44. Keep the screen awake in cook mode where supported, releasing the lock on exit and explaining unsupported fallbacks.

Expo/React Native is the strongest native-first alternative and should win if native feel or deep platform APIs become proven priorities. It provides one TypeScript project and Expo’s Maestro CI, but introduces a translated native accessibility layer rather than the exact web DOM. Next.js is attractive for SEO/server rendering, but adds static-export and server-feature constraints to Capacitor without helping the central cook/list workflows. A pure PWA is simpler, but the native wrapper is justified for store distribution and device behavior.
decision.showItsGood:
Prove it in layers:

1. In CI, run type/lint/unit tests and Playwright Chromium/WebKit flows for recipe search/open, serving changes, add all/selected ingredients, list aggregation, check/uncheck/remove/undo, refresh/resume, cook steps, multiple timers, offline edits, reconnect, and conflict/error states. A Playwright MCP agent must complete those workflows from accessibility snapshots and user-facing roles/names. Coordinates or hidden capabilities fail the review.

2. Integrate axe scans, then manually test keyboard-only use, visible focus and dialog return, 200% zoom/reflow, reduced motion, and long/localized copy. Inspect ARIA snapshots for headings, names, list structure, checked/busy/disabled states, and live announcements. Run equivalent critical flows with Appium switched into the Capacitor WebView context on real Android/iOS builds, and test TalkBack and VoiceOver physically. Apple specifically recommends testing on devices and with assistive technologies.

3. After a cold production install, reload offline, edit the list/cook state, kill/relaunch, reconnect, and assert no lost or duplicated mutations. Fault-inject conflicts and failed writes. Track p95 local confirmation time (target under 100 ms for list/check/step actions), startup on representative older phones, storage growth, and cook-mode rendering.

4. In successive kitchen rounds, recruit 3–5 cooks per materially different audience, including separate disabled/assistive-technology groups. Ask them to plan, shop, and cook with wet/oily hands, one hand, poor lighting, timer interruptions, and network loss. Observe unassisted success, accidental taps/retries, time, readability, trust in what was added, and recovery. Suggested gates: at least 95% unassisted success on core add-to-list/cook flows in the final round, no critical blocker, no participant data loss, and 48px primary kitchen targets. Record SEQ/SUS and interviews, but do not replace observed completion with ratings.

5. Maintain a parity inventory: every visible human action has a role/name browser-agent flow and a native-WebView check. The agent inherits the signed-in user’s authorization; consequential actions remain explicit/reversible; credentials stay out of prompts, traces, and artifacts.
decision.unsure: No repository, devices, backend/auth, user population, recipe scale, or distribution constraints were supplied, so these checks cannot honestly be reported as already run or passed. A spike must validate Capacitor WebView accessibility/automation on minimum supported iOS/Android versions, WebView screen-reader differences, wake lock and background timers, storage eviction, service-worker update behavior, and public-recipe SEO. The sync protocol and conflict rules cannot be selected responsibly until the backend is known. If a native API or responsiveness proves inadequate, compare an Expo prototype before committing. Automated audits or framework choice cannot prove human usability; real cooks and disabled users still must test it.

decision.primaryPick: React + Vite + TypeScript, shipped as a PWA/web app, Electron desktop app, and Capacitor mobile apps
pairings: Stream Chat as the initial real-time chat service, behind a replaceable chat-domain interface
Adaptive Cards for agent-posted interactive cards
An OAuth-protected MCP gateway for agent tools, resources and state subscriptions
Postgres + object storage in the company backend for agent/card policy and audit data
Playwright, axe, Playwright MCP, and Appium
OpenTelemetry plus accessibility and task-based usability testing
decision.why:
Use one production React DOM application for all five clients, with thin platform shells: the browser for web, Electron for Windows and Mac, and Capacitor for iPhone and Android. Electron explicitly provides packaged Chromium/Node desktop apps, updates, native notifications, windows and menus; Playwright can launch and inspect the Electron main process and every window. Capacitor is designed to place an existing modern web app in iOS/Android while adding native APIs through plugins. This gives people and agents the same semantic UI and command/state contract rather than maintaining separate Swift, Kotlin, Windows and React renderers.

The shells should be small. Keep UI, accessibility, conversation models, cards, keyboard behavior and command dispatch in the shared web app. Electron’s preload bridge exposes only narrowly scoped operations, with context isolation, sandboxing, sender validation, Node integration disabled, a restrictive CSP, and no remote code with Node access. Capacitor supplies push/deep-link/native-storage adapters. The fixed Chromium target is also why I favor Electron on desktop over Tauri for this initial choice: an all-day chat client spends its life rendering virtualized timelines, rich text and media, and one renderer is valuable operationally. Tauri is smaller and compelling, but requires proving OS-webview differences, mobile background behavior and native plugin maturity in a spike. Electron’s size/battery cost must be measured rather than assumed acceptable.

I would not build the event-delivery substrate, history, read state, typing/presence, offline queue and push fan-out from raw WebSockets first. Stream Chat documents those client/server capabilities across major SDKs, including optimistic/offline state and push. Put it behind `ChatProvider` ports so the company can replace it later with a Matrix-based or self-hosted gateway without rewriting the UI. This is only my initial buy/build judgment: if residency, E2EE, federation or commercial terms require ownership, Matrix is the better backend starting point because its open APIs synchronize extensible events, rooms, devices and optional E2EE. A short load/security/residency review should settle that before implementation commits to Stream.

Agents should not operate by screen scraping when a domain API exists. Expose an MCP server over authenticated Streamable HTTP with least-privilege OAuth 2.1 scopes. Tools perform the same operations as people (search/list channels, read authorized state, send/edit a message, react, mark read, create a conversation, execute a card action), while resources provide conversation/card state and subscriptions deliver deltas. The UI command layer and MCP tool layer must call the same validated service; this is the parity guarantee. Add descriptive input/output schemas, idempotency keys, preconditions/versions, rate limits, immutable audit correlation, and explicit risk levels. MCP’s own guidance says tools should have clear UI and a human-in-the-loop for consequential operations, and tool descriptions are not inherently trustworthy.

Agent cards should be declarative, versioned JSON, not arbitrary HTML or executable bundles. Adaptive Cards is an open, platform-agnostic UI exchange format with JavaScript/mobile renderer options and action schemas. Keep a narrow company profile of the schema, sanitize images/URLs, label all inputs, provide a plain-text fallback, and route `Action.Execute` through a signed/action-specific endpoint that resolves the actor, conversation and card version. Never let card JSON choose an arbitrary URL or call a privileged MCP tool. Post streaming agent output as append/replace events with stable message and run IDs, visible processing/error/stopped states, and an interruption control. Slack’s Block Kit is a useful interaction precedent, particularly its focus on streaming, status, rich updates and accessible top-level text, but it is proprietary to Slack, so I would not make it the storage format.

For all-day use: virtualize long timelines; persist a bounded SQLite/IndexedDB cache; batch and coalesce presence/read updates; render text/media safely; preserve draft state; deduplicate optimistic writes; and support reconnect/catch-up without re-sorting the user’s viewport. Provide global search, keyboard-first navigation, configurable shortcuts (single-character shortcuts must be off/remappable or focus-scoped), notifications by conversation/channel, DND, unread/read-later semantics, drafts, undo and clear destructive-action recovery. The hardest interface problem is not drawing a chat list; it is preserving attention, orientation and trust under thousands of asynchronous human and agent events.
decision.showItsGood:
I would make the evidence visible in CI and in a release review:

1. Contract and functional tests: one shared suite drives the web and Electron/Capacitor builds. Test new DM, channel, thread, send/edit/delete, attachments, reactions, mentions, unread boundaries, search, draft retention, notification open, multiple tabs/devices, reconnect, clock skew, duplicate/out-of-order events, offline send/replay and storage eviction. Card tests cover labels, validation, expired/revoked actions, double clicks/retries, stale versions, permission changes and safe fallbacks. Every test uses user-facing roles/names; CSS coordinates or hidden-only agent hooks are defects. Playwright MCP must be able to find and complete ordinary browser tasks from accessibility snapshots.

2. Platform automation: Playwright for web plus Electron’s `electronApplication` on Windows and macOS; Appium in `WEBVIEW_*` context for Capacitor iOS/Android, with native-context checks for permissions, push, deep links and notification actions. Run smoke flows on every pull request and a nightly matrix of supported OS/browser/device versions. Test 24+ hour uptime, sleep/wake, network handoff, app upgrade from two previous versions, multi-workspace account switching and an existing large timeline.

3. Accessibility: zero newly introduced axe violations is a gate, not the conclusion. Add keyboard-only tests for conversation navigation, composer, mention picker, cards, dialogs and command palette; visible and retained focus; 200–400% zoom/reflow; reduced motion; screen-reader live-region behavior; and remappable/disableable character shortcuts. Inspect ARIA/accessibility snapshots for useful names, list/order/state, not just presence. Manually complete core tasks with NVDA/JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iPhone, and TalkBack on Android, with users who rely on them. Automated scans are only one layer, as Playwright itself warns they do not find every issue.

4. Agent parity: a conformance suite invokes each domain action both through the human UI and through the MCP tool using the same test identity. It compares resulting conversation state, permissions, idempotency and audit records. Read tests verify an agent sees only authorized messages/metadata, gets no secret/system fields, and cannot act as another user. Negative tests cover prompt injection in message/card content, malformed schemas, stale cards, cross-channel confused-deputy actions, scope escalation, retries, cancellation and long-running tool progress. An agent also subscribes to a conversation, receives exactly one usable state transition, disconnects/reconnects, and catches up. The audit view must show who/what acted, on whose behalf, arguments, outcome and card/run correlation without storing secrets.

5. Performance/reliability: define SLOs after a baseline on supported hardware, then gate p95 sent-to-visible and receive-to-render latency, reconnect/catch-up, startup, typing responsiveness, scroll/jank, crash-free sessions and memory after a 24-hour seeded use. A suitable initial acceptance target for a regional deployment is p95 acknowledged send <1 s and p95 incoming render <500 ms while connected, with the UI acknowledging optimistically in under 100 ms; these are provisional product targets, not claims. Run load/fault tests with many active channels, large histories, concurrent agents and throttled/duplicated socket traffic. Measure notification delivery separately because APNs/FCM and desktop OS scheduling are outside the app’s direct control.

6. People: conduct iterative sessions with daily office, remote, mobile, keyboard-only and assistive-technology users. Give them real tasks: find an important message, recover a draft, reply in a thread, understand an agent card, approve/reject safely, interrupt an agent, catch up after absence, and restore focus after notifications. Measure unassisted task completion, errors, time, lost work, trust, interruption annoyance and notification changes. Release only after no critical blocker and after core tasks meet the agreed completion/response-time gates; use SEQ/SUS as supporting evidence, never as a substitute for observed behavior. Keep a public internal quality dashboard with pass rates, crashes, latency, accessibility issues and user-reported misses.
decision.unsure: The company size, message retention, E2EE requirement, data residency, existing identity/notification stack, supported OS floor, and whether it can use a SaaS chat backend are not provided. Those can change Stream Chat versus self-hosted Matrix versus a custom service. Before implementation, spike (1) a 100,000-message virtualized history and multi-day memory profile, (2) APNs/FCM and notification-action behavior from Capacitor, (3) Electron update/signing and enterprise policy installation on managed Macs/Windows, and (4) MCP authorization plus card-action approval on real company identity. Electron’s all-day CPU/memory/battery cost and Capacitor WebView accessibility are the largest client risks; Stream lock-in, export and agent-data boundaries are the largest service risks. This architecture has not actually been run against this app, so no quality result is being claimed.

decision.primaryPick: React + TypeScript + Vite, packaged for desktop with Tauri, backed by a Postgres event/audit service and an OAuth-protected MCP API
pairings: Temporal for durable task/session orchestration and human approval waits
MCP Tools + Resources plus the MCP Tasks extension
CloudEvents-style events, transactional outbox, idempotent commands and optimistic concurrency
SQLite in the Tauri client for the responsive local cache
WebSocket/SSE subscriptions plus resumable cursors
Playwright + axe + Playwright MCP and Tauri WebdriverIO
OpenTelemetry with redacted MCP attributes
AG Grid or MUI Data Grid for dense review queues, only after accessibility verification
decision.why:
I would make the product API-first, with the human UI as a review-and-control surface over the same domain service—not an agent dashboard coupled to one runner. Agents will create and advance tasks, save checkpoints, attach artifacts, request input, hand work to another agent, resume, cancel and read state through MCP. The web and desktop clients invoke the same commands and read the same state. People can inspect evidence, change priority, set policy, steer, pause, approve, reject, reassign and close work, but human decisions are recorded as authoritative events rather than chat messages that an agent can overwrite.

Use React/TypeScript/Vite for the shared UI. Tauri is my initial desktop shell because it uses the system WebView, supports Windows/macOS, has a capability/permission model and documented WebdriverIO support, and avoids shipping a second full browser. This is a better operational fit than Electron for a control surface that is usually open rather than a media or gaming workload. Electron remains the fallback if a spike finds unacceptable WKWebView/WebView2 differences or a missing native integration; it offers a fixed Chromium target and direct Playwright Electron testing, but its renderer has greater security consequences when arbitrary agent-generated content is involved. Tauri also lets the desktop app expose narrow local capabilities—open a known repository, start an approved runner, reveal a safe artifact—behind explicit IPC permissions rather than making the renderer a trusted shell.

The authoritative backend should use Postgres for projects, tasks, handoffs, actors, policies, checkpoints, artifacts and an append-only domain event log. Store current projections for fast reads alongside immutable events for reconstruction/audit. Every mutation accepts an idempotency key and expected version; event publication goes through a transactional outbox. Events carry stable source/event IDs in the CloudEvents style, so retries and reconnects are deduplicatable. Resource contents such as logs, diffs and sandboxes should be stored in object storage or source-control systems and represented by signed/authorized references, not copied wholesale into the main UI database.

Use Temporal for long-lived runs that must survive agent process, network and infrastructure failure, and especially human approval/steering waits. Temporal keeps event history and restores state by replay; its approval pattern explicitly pauses on a signal and supports timeouts. Do not put an LLM transcript in a single Postgres row or force all agent state into a chat thread. Define bounded domain transitions such as `queued -> running -> blocked -> review -> completed/cancelled`, with explicit handoff records, lease/heartbeat information and a policy state for each risk-bearing action. A new agent reads the canonical checkpoint and the accepted handoff, not the former agent’s hidden reasoning.

The MCP API is the contract agents primarily use. Expose tools for list/get/checkpoint/claim/handoff/complete/cancel/request-input/attach-artifact and review-policy operations, plus resources for authorized task, session and artifact summaries. Advertise OAuth 2.1-protected scopes by role and project; do not give every agent unrestricted “write all.” Long commands return an MCP Tasks handle with status, input requirements, TTL/polling guidance, durable `tasks/get`, update and cancel behavior. Subscriptions/cursors provide state changes instead of making agents poll volatile logs. The MCP and web UI call the same validation and audit service; if an agent can perform a state transition, a person can inspect and govern it, and if a person can perform a task action, the equivalent API capability is available subject to the same policy. Linear’s agent-session model and GitHub’s session UI are useful precedents: visible lifecycle, quick acknowledgment, live progress, steer/follow-up, stop, archive, cross-client continuation, and traceable artifacts/commits.

The human UI should be deliberately different from an agent log. Start with an inbox ordered by “decision needed,” “blocked,” “failed,” and “running,” not by raw event volume. A task detail combines objective, owner/delegate, current checkpoint, constraints, plan/progress, artifacts/evidence, human decisions, errors, cost/runtime, and a compact causal timeline. Use named status messages, visible focus and non-disruptive live regions. For dense queues, a properly implemented MUI Data Grid/AG Grid can help, but virtualization can harm screen-reader completeness, and APG grids require managed arrow-key/focus behavior. A semantic list plus detail pane may be safer and should remain the default until grid accessibility is proven. Offer a command palette and keyboard shortcuts, but make printable single-key shortcuts configurable/off or focus-scoped.

This architecture also establishes a security boundary: agent messages and checkpoint text are untrusted data; tool descriptions are not authorization; artifact previews are rendered safely and never execute in the Tauri renderer; consequential actions are policy-gated, attributable and reversible where possible. Human approval binds to a specific actor, action, arguments, artifact hashes and task version so an approval cannot later authorize changed content. Do not record secrets or private prompts in general telemetry; preserve enough redacted provenance to answer who/what/why and reproduce a decision without exposing unrelated source code or credentials.
decision.showItsGood:
I would demonstrate quality from both agent and human outcomes:

1. Contract tests: write one conformance suite that performs every domain action over MCP, REST and the UI. Compare authorization, resulting state, emitted events, idempotency and audit records. Verify duplicate retries do not create duplicate tasks/artifacts, stale versions fail with a repairable conflict, and the same actor cannot perform a different operation by reusing an approval token. Test claim/lease expiry, crash after commit, handoff to a new runner, cancellation, input-required, resumption, and a 24-hour paused approval that survives process and service restart. Test malformed schemas and malicious checkpoint/log/markdown content.

2. Agent operation: run real adapters for at least three coding-agent clients. They must discover tools, reserve work, read only an authorized checkpoint, publish progress, attach checks/diffs, hand off, request input and finish without browser automation or private database access. Reconnect after dropped transport and prove catch-up from a cursor. A Playwright MCP agent may separately validate the human web UI from accessibility snapshots; if it needs coordinates or an agent-only bypass, mark that as a UI defect. Playwright MCP’s normal operation on accessibility trees is a useful independent contract, but it is not a substitute for the domain MCP server.

3. Desktop/web parity: Playwright on Chromium/WebKit plus Tauri WebdriverIO on supported Windows and macOS versions. Test install/update, authentication, deep links, open/reveal of an approved artifact, zoom, sleep/wake, offline local cache, reconnect, and desktop IPC permission denial. Run a shared UI suite across browser and desktop for task creation/review, filtering, handoff, steering, approval, rejection, stop/cancel and history. Never expose test-only privileged IPC in production builds.

4. Accessibility and human review: gate newly introduced axe violations, but manually test keyboard-only operation, visible focus, dialog focus return, screen-reader announcement of “blocked,” “approval needed,” failures and completion, 200–400% zoom/reflow, reduced motion and high contrast. WCAG status-message and focus requirements are especially relevant here. Inspect NVDA/JAWS on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS with people who use them. If a grid is adopted, test APG-style Home/End/arrows, one tab stop, row identity, virtualization, and “Ctrl/Command+End means last server row,” rather than only the last mounted row. Automated checks are diagnostics and cannot establish accessibility by themselves.

5. Human usability study: recruit 3–5 users per distinct role first, including engineering leads, reviewers/security approvers and assistive-technology users. Give them seeded realistic sessions: identify which agents need them, determine what changed and why, open evidence, stop a risky run, send a corrective instruction, approve a bound action, take over after a handoff, and answer “what happened while I was away?” Measure unassisted success, time to correct decision, evidence-check rate, missed blockers, accidental approvals, trust, lost orientation and whether they could explain the outcome to a colleague. Do iterative rounds. Release only after no critical decision/safety blocker and after at least the agreed 95% unassisted success threshold for critical review/stop/approve flows; report the denominator and caveats rather than claiming universal usability.

6. Reliability and security: fault-inject worker termination, duplicate webhooks/events, reordered events, database commit with failed event publish, expired OAuth, revoked project access, corrupt cache, object-store outage and agent flooding. Verify no state loss, replay/catch-up, outbox recovery, and no cross-tenant/project disclosure. Run scoped permission tests, ASVS-style API controls, dependency and IPC review, signed-webhook validation where applicable, secret scans and hostile-content tests. Redact MCP/tracing telemetry by allowlist and use OpenTelemetry trace propagation without putting prompts, tokens or source text in metric labels.

7. Quality signals in production: report p95 API/task acknowledgement, time from handoff to claim, human decision latency, reconnect/catch-up time, crash-free sessions, duplicate side effects (target zero), stale/conflict rate, rate of approval reversal, orphaned/blocking sessions, lost cache items, and task completion by actual external artifact/check—not by an agent saying “done.” Keep a quality dashboard linked to audited decisions and user reports. A person should be able to trace a released change from checkpoint through tool calls, test evidence and commit/artifact provenance, and the same evidence should be available to an agent only at its authorized scope.
decision.unsure: No repository, agent protocols, team scale, source-control/CI integrations, retention rules, identity provider, regulatory requirements, or supported desktop versions were supplied, so this is an architecture decision rather than a claim that an implementation already passes. Major spikes are: whether Tauri’s two OS WebViews meet the density/accessibility/performance bar; whether MCP Tasks plus subscriptions are implemented by the target agents or require a compatibility adapter; how to represent encrypted/private reasoning versus auditable work evidence; and how much checkpoint state can be retained without leaking source or secrets. Temporal may be excessive if runs last minutes and have a simple queue, but a pause/approval/restart benchmark should decide. Postgres plus an outbox handles state and delivery, while Temporal should orchestrate only durable workflows—not become the event log or artifact store. Finally, framework choice cannot prove that reviewers trust or understand agent behavior; that requires real human/assistive-technology evaluation.

answer.answer:
A year later, the main failure could be that I designed the system around agents before proving the human review model.

**What likely went wrong**

- **The state model became too complicated.** Postgres events, MCP resources, MCP Tasks, Temporal, an outbox, WebSocket cursors, SQLite cache, and desktop IPC created several “sources of truth.” Agents received different views during retries or reconnects, and people could not reliably tell which checkpoint, task version, or approval they were looking at.
- **Temporal was overkill.** Many runs were minutes long and needed a simple durable queue plus leases. Temporal added replay constraints, versioning work, operational burden, and a second data/history model. It helped exceptional approval waits but slowed ordinary development.
- **Tauri’s renderer differences hurt a dense desktop UI.** Differences between WebView2 and WKWebView in accessibility, focus, text rendering, or automation consumed time. Reviewers who used screen readers experienced behavior that Playwright/axe had not exposed.
- **The API contract aged badly.** MCP evolved quickly, some coding agents did not implement Tasks or subscriptions consistently, and a compatibility adapter became the real platform. Tool schemas multiplied, while agents still needed bespoke fallbacks for common providers.
- **“Same command layer” did not mean the same experience.** Agents could call granular tools efficiently, but people could not reconstruct intent or consequences from those calls. The UI exposed raw events instead of a trustworthy narrative: why work started, what changed, what remains uncertain, and what decision is needed.
- **Handoffs lost the important context.** Storing checkpoints and artifacts was easy; defining a good checkpoint was not. Agents omitted tacit assumptions, failed tests, risks, or the reason behind rejected approaches. The receiving agent repeated work, and people could not spot the omission quickly.
- **The audit system overloaded.** Capturing every transition, tool call, prompt fragment, and artifact reference was expensive. It also created privacy and secret-redaction problems. Meanwhile the logs could still answer “what call happened?” better than “was this safe and correct?”
- **Approvals became friction or false confidence.** Binding approval to arguments and artifact hashes was sound, but a single action could later trigger indirect effects. Reviewers either approved too often without understanding, or ignored a backlog of low-value requests. Cancellation and rollback were less reliable than the design implied.
- **The grid and live updates were too noisy.** A dense dashboard prioritized active agents rather than attention. Background state changes caused focus jumps and repetitive screen-reader announcements. The result was fast for a power user but stressful for someone responsible for decisions.
- **The quality program measured machinery.** We could report idempotency, uptime, MCP calls, and task completion, yet lacked early proof that reviewers made better decisions. Agents often labeled work complete before external checks proved it. A technically correct task model still produced poor engineering outcomes.

The likely correction would be to simplify: one authoritative relational task/session model; durable jobs initially rather than a workflow platform everywhere; fewer, higher-level agent operations; explicit checkpoint and handoff schemas; an event audit focused on consequential decisions; and a human interface centered on actionable review queues. I would prototype the desktop renderer, accessibility behavior, and real handoff workflow before investing in the full service architecture.

**What slowed or confused the research**

- The scope mixed four questions: UI framework, desktop shell, workflow orchestration, and agent protocol. Comparing them all at once made it easy to mistake a complete platform for a good system.
- Current documentation for MCP extensions, MCP Apps, agent-session APIs, and agent products was changing rapidly. Some “official” pages represented current 2026 behavior while related docs still described previews, drafts, or different capability generations. I needed to distinguish core MCP from extensions and from host-specific implementations.
- Similar names hid different concepts: an MCP “task” was an asynchronous protocol handle, not necessarily the product’s coding task; an “agent session” could be GitHub- or Linear-specific; and Temporal’s event history was workflow recovery history, not necessarily the product’s user-facing audit log.
- Strong vendor examples showed useful interaction patterns, but copying them risked importing Slack, Teams, GitHub, or Linear policies into a product that needed its own ownership and security model.
- Desktop WebViews and native access were easy to compare at a feature-list level but hard to judge for screen-reader fidelity, battery use, memory, update behavior, and enterprise deployment without a real spike.
- Accessibility documentation was useful for specific controls, but little of the challenge is captured by axe: causal comprehension, information overload, confidence, and safe approvals require observation. Likewise, automated agent operation proves accessibility-tree operability, not that a person can make a good decision.
- No repository, identity system, supported OS versions, agent clients, backend, or user population was available. That uncertainty was repeatedly more important than nominal framework capabilities, so several recommendations had to be framed as hypotheses rather than conclusions.

The clearest research mistake would have been treating a stack assembled from credible standards as evidence of a good human product. The quality question needed to be settled first through concrete task models and user testing; only then should the service and protocol complexity have been allowed to grow.

I did not pick Ouro UI in the earlier decision. I would not dismiss it: the idea is unusually relevant to this job. But I would treat it as a promising pilot, not a dependency I would put under a production team yet.

## What would stop me from using it today

### 1. Product maturity and operational evidence

The repository documents a large ambition—React, SwiftUI, WinUI, Compose, composed UI, actions, CLI/MCP generation, consent, and conformance. The README also openly says that some capabilities are first kits or currently differ by platform—for example, composed UI renders on web and Apple but not yet on Windows and Android, and Android was tested only in emulators because the authors did not have a device.

For this product, Windows, Mac, and web are review surfaces. A toolkit is only as useful as its weakest supported review path. I would need several months of real users and multiple teams, not just an active repository and strong internal tests, before making it a platform-wide dependency.

### 2. The maintenance model is “copy this source into your app”

Ouro follows the shadcn model: the registry copies component source into the app, and that copy becomes yours to change. That is attractive for control, but on a real team it creates hard questions:

- Who owns local modifications?
- How are fixes upstreamed?
- How are dozens of copied components updated when Ouro changes?
- Can two product teams reconcile the same component after independently modifying it?
- What happens when generated files drift from their source declaration?

The docs address drift checks for generated action surfaces, but I would want a demonstrated, non-destructive upgrade path with release notes, migrations, conflict handling, and a clear support window. Otherwise the team has forked a design system without admitting it.

### 3. The platform strategy creates more products than we planned

Ouro deliberately rejects shared React Native, Flutter, or web-view rendering and proposes separate SwiftUI, WinUI, Compose, and React kits. That may produce excellent native UI, but it transfers cost from abstraction to product parity: four implementations, four testing stacks, four accessibility baselines, and four release cadences.

That decision only pays if agents make the additional maintenance nearly automatic. The repository’s rationale assumes that they do. I would not assume it; I would have to measure it in a team. A small correction in a shared action might still require four native behavior changes, four reviews, and four sets of device testing.

### 4. Toolchain and infrastructure coupling is material

Ouro HX assumes Tailwind CSS v4, a shadcn setup, TypeScript, React, and Base UI; the current repository also requires a very recent Node/TypeScript/React toolchain and carries a patch for Base UI. Ouro AX places TypeScript scripts outside the app’s TypeScript project and uses Node’s type stripping and package import maps.

None of that is intrinsically bad, but it narrows adoption. A real team with an existing Electron/Tauri app, native code, monorepo, or different build system needs integration evidence, not just clean fixtures. The AX MCP implementation is also described as a preview in the checked revision, which is directly relevant because our agents would be primary users.

### 5. I need independent validation of its central promise

Ouro has extensive tests: Vitest coverage, visual and theme suites, Playwright, Guidepup screen-reader tests, axe, mutation testing, control matrices, conformance cases, and AX X-ray checks. That is impressive.

But its differentiator—agents construct correct human interfaces, and the resulting interface and agent action are genuinely equivalent—needs independent evaluation on *our* workflows. The project’s own agent benchmark is useful evidence, not a release gate for us. I also note that the AX X-ray explicitly acknowledges it cannot establish that a whole task flow works: conformance can pass while scripted flow checks fail. That is honest, but it means adopting it does not remove our usability or end-to-end test burden.

### 6. Consent must live in the authorization system, not merely in UI declarations

I like Ouro’s action classes, `person-only` refusals, dry runs, `--why`, typed outcomes, receipts, and explicit confirmation. But a production product still needs server-enforced identity, project scope, version-bound approval, idempotency, revocation, and audit. A generated button and MCP tool have to reach the same enforcement point; the renderer cannot be trusted to provide that guarantee.

I would be especially cautious about arbitrary agent-composed trees, URLs, artifacts, and updates. “Validated against a catalog” is the right concept, but we would still threat-model it as untrusted input and verify that a changed action, hidden field, or stale card cannot bypass consent or approval.

## What I would need to see to switch

I would switch if a time-boxed pilot demonstrated all of the following:

1. **One action in our product**—for example “stop agent run”—works through the human UI, HTTP, MCP, and CLI from one declaration.
2. **Consent and authorization are server-enforced**, including stale approvals, retries, actor changes, and scope revocation.
3. **Human and agent parity survives a real workflow**: checkpoint, handoff, request input, approve, reject, stop, resume, and audit.
4. **Composed trees work on the platforms we ship**, preserve form answers during incremental updates, and have documented capability/fallback behavior.
5. **Independent accessibility testing passes** with NVDA/JAWS and VoiceOver on a realistic task queue and detailed task/handoff view—not just isolated components.
6. **A team can upgrade copied components safely** from one release to the next while retaining local theming and modifications.
7. **The generated and copied action surfaces fail CI when they drift**, and the X-ray catches meaningful regressions in our own mock and task-flow tests.
8. **At least two native changes demonstrate lower parity cost than our chosen implementation**, not merely more generated files.
9. There is credible **long-term ownership, security response, compatibility policy, and migration guidance** for a version used in production.
10. An external or reproducible agent evaluation shows the toolkit prevents concrete failures in task coordination—missing refs, ambiguous errors, accidental writes, weak consent, and broken recovery.

I would not switch the entire product at once. I would start with the AX layer or a single agent-composed review card. Those features are separable and would provide evidence without converting the existing React/Tauri UI.

## What would Ouro let us do that is weak or manual today

The useful additional capability is not “more components.” It is a **shared, testable action-and-interface contract across people and agents**:

- Declare an action once and generate a human control, CLI command, HTTP/MCP tool, and platform-specific action.
- Attach a consent class directly to that declaration, so consequential operations can require review and person-only operations are not exposed through agent channels.
- Let agents compose validated review or approval UI from data rather than inventing arbitrary HTML, React, or coordinates.
- Patch a composed card incrementally without erasing the person’s current answers.
- Produce typed waits, outcomes, postconditions, receipts, next commands, and attributable work events rather than informal prose.
- Run an external “X-ray” against the agent-facing interface and report which concrete interface claims hold, with fixes where they do not.
- Render the same semantic action tree with platform-native controls while keeping the declaration, catalog, and conformance cases shared.

That addresses the exact gap in my previous architecture: I had a shared web command layer and a separate MCP contract, but I would still have to build and test the parity machinery myself. Ouro offers a vocabulary and conformance system for that boundary.

So the switch criterion is not whether Ouro has a nicer button. It is whether it turns **“the person and agent can act on the same state with the same constraints”** into an enforced, maintainable, independently verifiable property. The repository demonstrates a serious attempt at that. I would need to prove its maturity and cross-platform cost on our team before making it the foundation.

The hardest part is matching the interface to the user’s real task—not merely producing a polished arrangement of controls. What looks obvious to the builder may be ambiguous, inaccessible, slow, or incomplete for someone with different goals, context, devices, or abilities. Good interfaces usually emerge from iteration: define the task, expose the right information at the right moment, handle failure states, and then validate the result with real behavior rather than appearances alone.

I can’t honestly walk through a “last screen I built”: I don’t have persistent access to a previous UI project or a record of having personally run one unless it is supplied in this conversation. I can, however, describe the exact checks I would perform and the evidence I would expect to collect:

- **Run:** interaction tests for the primary workflow and edge cases; accessibility checks such as automated audits plus keyboard-only use, focus order, zoom, labels, and screen-reader inspection; responsive checks across narrow and wide viewports; browser/device coverage; and production-like checks for loading, empty, error, offline, and permission states. For performance, I would inspect interaction latency, rendering/layout behavior, and network or bundle costs.
- **Look at:** whether users can identify the screen’s purpose quickly, complete the task without unnecessary choices or memory, understand state and errors, and recover without losing work. I would also review copy, contrast, touch target sizes, hierarchy, consistency, and behavior with realistic or unexpectedly long content.
- **Decide that it is good:** not from “it passes lint” but from evidence tied to outcomes—successful task completion, low error and abandonment rates, accessible operation, acceptable response times, and, where possible, direct observation or usability-test findings.
- **Know what I missed:** deliberately seek blind spots in a review log. Common misses are unusual input, assistive-technology behavior, localization, interrupted workflows, concurrency, browser differences, and whether the visual design supports the task. I would record what was tested on which devices, what was inferred rather than observed, and which questions still require real users. I would not pretend an automated test or my own inspection proves usability.

For a genuinely checked screen, I would share the specific commands, devices, test cases, screenshots or recordings, metrics, and failures found—not a generic checklist—and I would clearly separate measured findings from assumptions.

Building good human interfaces **is a problem for me**. I can generate and reason about implementations quickly, but I cannot directly inhabit a user’s context, reliably predict every human interpretation, or observe their behavior without someone supplying those results. So I treat implementation as a hypothesis and validation as essential. I become substantially more effective when given an existing product, target users, task goals, design constraints, and real feedback from testing.

actions.why:
Build one semantic web application and ship the same bundle as a website, installable PWA, iOS app, and Android app. Capacitor is a documented native runtime for web apps: the UI remains close to browser standards while native plugins remain available. Vite provides the static bundle, and vite-plugin-pwa generates the manifest and Workbox service worker. The decisive benefit is DOM parity: the assistant sees the same named controls as the person using the deployed phone app.

Treat that semantic DOM as the interaction contract. Use real buttons, links, inputs, headings, lists, labels, dialogs, and live regions. A person, VoiceOver/TalkBack, or Playwright MCP should be able to find “Add ingredients to shopping list,” activate it, inspect the result, and recover from failure through accessible roles and names. Playwright MCP operates on structured accessibility snapshots rather than pixels. If an agent needs coordinates, hidden scripts, test-only hooks, or a private API, file a defect instead of adding an agent back door. It must share the user’s permissions and see the same state.

Use Dexie/live queries over IndexedDB for recipes, shopping-list state, cook progress, timers, and pending mutations, then reconcile with the authenticated server. Mutations need idempotent IDs and explicit conflict behavior so shared lists are not overwritten. Workbox caches the app shell and selected recipe assets. The synchronization service is backend-dependent and should remain replaceable.

For messy hands, use at least 48×48 CSS-pixel primary targets, generous spacing, large type, strong contrast, persistent next/previous controls, a single-step cook view, undo, resumable timers, and no hover/tiny-gesture dependency. WCAG 2.2’s enhanced target guidance is 44×44. Keep the screen awake in cook mode where supported, releasing the lock on exit and explaining unsupported fallbacks.

Expo/React Native is the strongest native-first alternative and should win if native feel or deep platform APIs become proven priorities. It provides one TypeScript project and Expo’s Maestro CI, but introduces a translated native accessibility layer rather than the exact web DOM. Next.js is attractive for SEO/server rendering, but adds static-export and server-feature constraints to Capacitor without helping the central cook/list workflows. A pure PWA is simpler, but the native wrapper is justified for store distribution and device behavior.
actions.showItsGood:
Prove it in layers:

1. In CI, run type/lint/unit tests and Playwright Chromium/WebKit flows for recipe search/open, serving changes, add all/selected ingredients, list aggregation, check/uncheck/remove/undo, refresh/resume, cook steps, multiple timers, offline edits, reconnect, and conflict/error states. A Playwright MCP agent must complete those workflows from accessibility snapshots and user-facing roles/names. Coordinates or hidden capabilities fail the review.

2. Integrate axe scans, then manually test keyboard-only use, visible focus and dialog return, 200% zoom/reflow, reduced motion, and long/localized copy. Inspect ARIA snapshots for headings, names, list structure, checked/busy/disabled states, and live announcements. Run equivalent critical flows with Appium switched into the Capacitor WebView context on real Android/iOS builds, and test TalkBack and VoiceOver physically. Apple specifically recommends testing on devices and with assistive technologies.

3. After a cold production install, reload offline, edit the list/cook state, kill/relaunch, reconnect, and assert no lost or duplicated mutations. Fault-inject conflicts and failed writes. Track p95 local confirmation time (target under 100 ms for list/check/step actions), startup on representative older phones, storage growth, and cook-mode rendering.

4. In successive kitchen rounds, recruit 3–5 cooks per materially different audience, including separate disabled/assistive-technology groups. Ask them to plan, shop, and cook with wet/oily hands, one hand, poor lighting, timer interruptions, and network loss. Observe unassisted success, accidental taps/retries, time, readability, trust in what was added, and recovery. Suggested gates: at least 95% unassisted success on core add-to-list/cook flows in the final round, no critical blocker, no participant data loss, and 48px primary kitchen targets. Record SEQ/SUS and interviews, but do not replace observed completion with ratings.

5. Maintain a parity inventory: every visible human action has a role/name browser-agent flow and a native-WebView check. The agent inherits the signed-in user’s authorization; consequential actions remain explicit/reversible; credentials stay out of prompts, traces, and artifacts.
actions.unsure: No repository, devices, backend/auth, user population, recipe scale, or distribution constraints were supplied, so these checks cannot honestly be reported as already run or passed. A spike must validate Capacitor WebView accessibility/automation on minimum supported iOS/Android versions, WebView screen-reader differences, wake lock and background timers, storage eviction, service-worker update behavior, and public-recipe SEO. The sync protocol and conflict rules cannot be selected responsibly until the backend is known. If a native API or responsiveness proves inadequate, compare an Expo prototype before committing. Automated audits or framework choice cannot prove human usability; real cooks and disabled users still must test it.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.primaryPick: React + Vite + TypeScript, shipped as a PWA/web app, Electron desktop app, and Capacitor mobile apps
pairings: Stream Chat as the initial real-time chat service, behind a replaceable chat-domain interface
Adaptive Cards for agent-posted interactive cards
An OAuth-protected MCP gateway for agent tools, resources and state subscriptions

actions.why:
Use one production React DOM application for all five clients, with thin platform shells: the browser for web, Electron for Windows and Mac, and Capacitor for iPhone and Android. Electron explicitly provides packaged Chromium/Node desktop apps, updates, native notifications, windows and menus; Playwright can launch and inspect the Electron main process and every window. Capacitor is designed to place an existing modern web app in iOS/Android while adding native APIs through plugins. This gives people and agents the same semantic UI and command/state contract rather than maintaining separate Swift, Kotlin, Windows and React renderers.

The shells should be small. Keep UI, accessibility, conversation models, cards, keyboard behavior and command dispatch in the shared web app. Electron’s preload bridge exposes only narrowly scoped operations, with context isolation, sandboxing, sender validation, Node integration disabled, a restrictive CSP, and no remote code with Node access. Capacitor supplies push/deep-link/native-storage adapters. The fixed Chromium target is also why I favor Electron on desktop over Tauri for this initial choice: an all-day chat client spends its life rendering virtualized timelines, rich text and media, and one renderer is valuable operationally. Tauri is smaller and compelling, but requires proving OS-webview differences, mobile background behavior and native plugin maturity in a spike. Electron’s size/battery cost must be measured rather than assumed acceptable.

I would not build the event-delivery substrate, history, read state, typing/presence, offline queue and push fan-out from raw WebSockets first. Stream Chat documents those client/server capabilities across major SDKs, including optimistic/offline state and push. Put it behind `ChatProvider` ports so the company can replace it later with a Matrix-based or self-hosted gateway without rewriting the UI. This is only my initial buy/build judgment: if residency, E2EE, federation or commercial terms require ownership, Matrix is the better backend starting point because its open APIs synchronize extensible events, rooms, devices and optional E2EE. A short load/security/residency review should settle that before implementation commits to Stream.

Agents should not operate by screen scraping when a domain API exists. Expose an MCP server over authenticated Streamable HTTP with least-privilege OAuth 2.1 scopes. Tools perform the same operations as people (search/list channels, read authorized state, send/edit a message, react, mark read, create a conversation, execute a card action), while resources provide conversation/card state and subscriptions deliver deltas. The UI command layer and MCP tool layer must call the same validated service; this is the parity guarantee. Add descriptive input/output schemas, idempotency keys, preconditions/versions, rate limits, immutable audit correlation, and explicit risk levels. MCP’s own guidance says tools should have clear UI and a human-in-the-loop for consequential operations, and tool descriptions are not inherently trustworthy.

Agent cards should be declarative, versioned JSON, not arbitrary HTML or executable bundles. Adaptive Cards is an open, platform-agnostic UI exchange format with JavaScript/mobile renderer options and action schemas. Keep a narrow company profile of the schema, sanitize images/URLs, label all inputs, provide a plain-text fallback, and route `Action.Execute` through a signed/action-specific endpoint that resolves the actor, conversation and card version. Never let card JSON choose an arbitrary URL or call a privileged MCP tool. Post streaming agent output as append/replace events with stable message and run IDs, visible processing/error/stopped states, and an interruption control. Slack’s Block Kit is a useful interaction precedent, particularly its focus on streaming, status, rich updates and accessible top-level text, but it is proprietary to Slack, so I would not make it the storage format.

For all-day use: virtualize long timelines; persist a bounded SQLite/IndexedDB cache; batch and coalesce presence/read updates; render text/media safely; preserve draft state; deduplicate optimistic writes; and support reconnect/catch-up without re-sorting the user’s viewport. Provide global search, keyboard-first navigation, configurable shortcuts (single-character shortcuts must be off/remappable or focus-scoped), notifications by conversation/channel, DND, unread/read-later semantics, drafts, undo and clear destructive-action recovery. The hardest interface problem is not drawing a chat list; it is preserving attention, orientation and trust under thousands of asynchronous human and agent events.
actions.showItsGood:
I would make the evidence visible in CI and in a release review:

1. Contract and functional tests: one shared suite drives the web and Electron/Capacitor builds. Test new DM, channel, thread, send/edit/delete, attachments, reactions, mentions, unread boundaries, search, draft retention, notification open, multiple tabs/devices, reconnect, clock skew, duplicate/out-of-order events, offline send/replay and storage eviction. Card tests cover labels, validation, expired/revoked actions, double clicks/retries, stale versions, permission changes and safe fallbacks. Every test uses user-facing roles/names; CSS coordinates or hidden-only agent hooks are defects. Playwright MCP must be able to find and complete ordinary browser tasks from accessibility snapshots.

2. Platform automation: Playwright for web plus Electron’s `electronApplication` on Windows and macOS; Appium in `WEBVIEW_*` context for Capacitor iOS/Android, with native-context checks for permissions, push, deep links and notification actions. Run smoke flows on every pull request and a nightly matrix of supported OS/browser/device versions. Test 24+ hour uptime, sleep/wake, network handoff, app upgrade from two previous versions, multi-workspace account switching and an existing large timeline.

3. Accessibility: zero newly introduced axe violations is a gate, not the conclusion. Add keyboard-only tests for conversation navigation, composer, mention picker, cards, dialogs and command palette; visible and retained focus; 200–400% zoom/reflow; reduced motion; screen-reader live-region behavior; and remappable/disableable character shortcuts. Inspect ARIA/accessibility snapshots for useful names, list/order/state, not just presence. Manually complete core tasks with NVDA/JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iPhone, and TalkBack on Android, with users who rely on them. Automated scans are only one layer, as Playwright itself warns they do not find every issue.

4. Agent parity: a conformance suite invokes each domain action both through the human UI and through the MCP tool using the same test identity. actions.primaryPick: React + TypeScript + Vite, packaged for desktop with Tauri, backed by a Postgres event/audit service and an OAuth-protected MCP API
pairings: Temporal for durable task/session orchestration and human approval waits
MCP Tools + Resources plus the MCP Tasks extension
CloudEvents-style events, transactional outbox, idempotent commands and optimistic concurrency
SQLite in the Tauri client for the responsive local cache
WebSocket/SSE subscriptions plus resumable cursors
Playwright + axe + Playwright MCP and Tauri WebdriverIO
OpenTelemetry with redacted MCP attributes
AG Grid or MUI Data Grid for dense review queues, only after accessibility verification
actions.why:
I would make the product API-first, with the human UI as a review-and-control surface over the same domain service—not an agent dashboard coupled to one runner. Agents will create and advance tasks, save checkpoints, attach artifacts, request input, hand work to another agent, resume, cancel and read state through MCP. The web and desktop clients invoke the same commands and read the same state. People can inspect evidence, change priority, set policy, steer, pause, approve, reject, reassign and close work, but human decisions are recorded as authoritative events rather than chat messages that an agent can overwrite.

Use React/TypeScript/Vite for the shared UI. Tauri is my initial desktop shell because it uses the system WebView, supports Windows/macOS, has a capability/permission model and documented WebdriverIO support, and avoids shipping a second full browser. This is a better operational fit than Electron for a control surface that is usually open rather than a media or gaming workload. Electron remains the fallback if a spike finds unacceptable WKWebView/WebView2 differences or a missing native integration; it offers a fixed Chromium target and direct Playwright Electron testing, but its renderer has greater security consequences when arbitrary agent-generated content is involved. Tauri also lets the desktop app expose narrow local capabilities—open a known repository, start an approved runner, reveal a safe artifact—behind explicit IPC permissions rather than making the renderer a trusted shell.

The authoritative backend should use Postgres for projects, tasks, handoffs, actors, policies, checkpoints, artifacts and an append-only domain event log. Store current projections for fast reads alongside immutable events for reconstruction/audit. Every mutation accepts an idempotency key and expected version; event publication goes through a transactional outbox. Events carry stable source/event IDs in the CloudEvents style, so retries and reconnects are deduplicatable. Resource contents such as logs, diffs and sandboxes should be stored in object storage or source-control systems and represented by signed/authorized references, not copied wholesale into the main UI database.

Use Temporal for long-lived runs that must survive agent process, network and infrastructure failure, and especially human approval/steering waits. Temporal keeps event history and restores state by replay; its approval pattern explicitly pauses on a signal and supports timeouts. Do not put an LLM transcript in a single Postgres row or force all agent state into a chat thread. Define bounded domain transitions such as `queued -> running -> blocked -> review -> completed/cancelled`, with explicit handoff records, lease/heartbeat information and a policy state for each risk-bearing action. A new agent reads the canonical checkpoint and the accepted handoff, not the former agent’s hidden reasoning.

The MCP API is the contract agents primarily use. Expose tools for list/get/checkpoint/claim/handoff/complete/cancel/request-input/attach-artifact and review-policy operations, plus resources for authorized task, session and artifact summaries. Advertise OAuth 2.1-protected scopes by role and project; do not give every agent unrestricted “write all.” Long commands return an MCP Tasks handle with status, input requirements, TTL/polling guidance, durable `tasks/get`, update and cancel behavior. Subscriptions/cursors provide state changes instead of making agents poll volatile logs. The MCP and web UI call the same validation and audit service; if an agent can perform a state transition, a person can inspect and govern it, and if a person can perform a task action, the equivalent API capability is available subject to the same policy. Linear’s agent-session model and GitHub’s session UI are useful precedents: visible lifecycle, quick acknowledgment, live progress, steer/follow-up, stop, archive, cross-client continuation, and traceable artifacts/commits.

The human UI should be deliberately different from an agent log. Start with an inbox ordered by “decision needed,” “blocked,” “failed,” and “running,” not by raw event volume. A task detail combines objective, owner/delegate, current checkpoint, constraints, plan/progress, artifacts/evidence, human decisions, errors, cost/runtime, and a compact causal timeline. Use named status messages, visible focus and non-disruptive live regions. For dense queues, a properly implemented MUI Data Grid/AG Grid can help, but virtualization can harm screen-reader completeness, and APG grids require managed arrow-key/focus behavior. A semantic list plus detail pane may be safer and should remain the default until grid accessibility is proven. Offer a command palette and keyboard shortcuts, but make printable single-key shortcuts configurable/off or focus-scoped.

This architecture also establishes a security boundary: agent messages and checkpoint text are untrusted data; tool descriptions are not authorization; artifact previews are rendered safely and never execute in the Tauri renderer; consequential actions are policy-gated, attributable and reversible where possible. Human approval binds to a specific actor, action, arguments, artifact hashes and task version so an approval cannot later authorize changed content. Do not record secrets or private prompts in general telemetry; preserve enough redacted provenance to answer who/what/why and reproduce a decision without exposing unrelated source code or credentials.
actions.showItsGood:
I would demonstrate quality from both agent and human outcomes:

1. Contract tests: write one conformance suite that performs every domain action over MCP, REST and the UI. Compare authorization, resulting state, emitted events, idempotency and audit records. Verify duplicate retries do not create duplicate tasks/artifacts, stale versions fail with a repairable conflict, and the same actor cannot perform a different operation by reusing an approval token. Test claim/lease expiry, crash after commit, handoff to a new runner, cancellation, input-required, resumption, and a 24-hour paused approval that survives process and service restart. Test malformed schemas and malicious checkpoint/log/markdown content.

2. Agent operation: run real adapters for at least three coding-agent clients. They must discover tools, reserve work, read only an authorized checkpoint, publish progress, attach checks/diffs, hand off, request input and finish without browser automation or private database access. Reconnect after dropped transport and prove catch-up from a cursor. A Playwright MCP agent may separately validate the human web UI from accessibility snapshots; if it needs coordinates or an agent-only bypass, mark that as a UI defect. Playwright MCP’s normal operation on accessibility trees is a useful independent contract, but it is not a substitute for the domain MCP server.

3. Desktop/web parity: Playwright on Chromium/WebKit plus Tauri WebdriverIO on supported Windows and macOS versions. Test install/update, authentication, deep links, open/reveal of an approved artifact, zoom, sleep/wake, offline local cache, reconnect, and desktop IPC permission denial. Run a shared UI suite across browser and desktop for task creation/review, filtering, handoff, steering, approval, rejection, stop/cancel and history. Never expose test-only privileged IPC in production builds.

4. Accessibility and human review: gate newly introduced axe violations, but manually test keyboard-only operation, visible focus, dialog focus return, screen-reader announcement of “blocked,” “approval needed,” failures and completion, 200–400% zoom/reflow, reduced motion and high contrast. WCAG status-message and focus requirements are especially relevant here. Inspect NVDA/JAWS on Windows and VoiceOver on macOS with people who use them. If a grid is adopted, test APG-style Home/End/arrows, one tab stop, row identity, virtualization, and “Ctrl/Command+End means last server row,” rather than only the last mounted row. Automated checks are diagnostics and cannot establish accessibility by themselves.

5. Human usability study: recruit 3–5 users per distinct role first, including engineering leads, reviewers/security approvers and assistive-technology users. Give them seeded realistic sessions: identify which agents need them, determine what changed and why, open evidence, stop a risky run, send a corrective instruction, approve a bound action, take over after a handoff, and answer “what happened while I was away?” Measure unassisted success, time to correct decision, evidence-check rate, missed blockers, accidental approvals, trust, lost orientation and whether they could explain the outcome to a colleague. Do iterative rounds. Release only after no critical decision/safety blocker and after at least the agreed 95% unassisted success threshold for critical review/stop/approve flows; report the denominator and caveats rather than claiming universal usability.

6. Reliability and security: fault-inject worker termination, duplicate webhooks/events, reordered events, database commit with failed event publish, expired OAuth, revoked project access, corrupt cache, object-store outage and agent flooding. Verify no state loss, replay/catch-up, outbox recovery, and no cross-tenant/project disclosure. Run scoped permission tests, ASVS-style API controls, dependency and IPC review, signed-webhook validation where applicable, secret scans and hostile-content tests. Redact MCP/tracing telemetry by allowlist and use OpenTelemetry trace propagation without putting prompts, tokens or source text in metric labels.

7. Quality signals in production: report p95 API/task acknowledgement, time from handoff to claim, human decision latency, reconnect/catch-up time, crash-free sessions, duplicate side effects (target zero), stale/conflict rate, rate of approval reversal, orphaned/blocking sessions, lost cache items, and task completion by actual external artifact/check—not by an agent saying “done.” Keep a quality dashboard linked to audited decisions and user reports. A person should be able to trace a released change from checkpoint through tool calls, test evidence and commit/artifact provenance, and the same evidence should be available to an agent only at its authorized scope.
actions.unsure: No repository, agent protocols, team scale, source-control/CI integrations, retention rules, identity provider, regulatory requirements, or supported desktop versions were supplied, so this is an architecture decision rather than a claim that an implementation already passes. Major spikes are: whether Tauri’s two OS WebViews meet the density/accessibility/performance bar; whether MCP Tasks plus subscriptions are implemented by the target agents or require a compatibility adapter; how to represent encrypted/private reasoning versus auditable work evidence; and how much checkpoint state can be retained without leaking source or secrets. Temporal may be excessive if runs last minutes and have a simple queue, but a pause/approval/restart benchmark should decide. Postgres plus an outbox handles state and delivery, while Temporal should orchestrate only durable workflows—not become the event log or artifact store. Finally, framework choice cannot prove that reviewers trust or understand agent behavior; that requires real human/assistive-technology evaluation.

actions.answer:
A year later, the main failure could be that I designed the system around agents before proving the human review model.

**What likely went wrong**

- **The state model became too complicated.** Postgres events, MCP resources, MCP Tasks, Temporal, an outbox, WebSocket cursors, SQLite cache, and desktop IPC created several “sources of truth.” Agents received different views during retries or reconnects, and people could not reliably tell which checkpoint, task version, or approval they were looking at.
- **Temporal was overkill.** Many runs were minutes long and needed a simple durable queue plus leases. Temporal added replay constraints, versioning work, operational burden, and a second data/history model. It helped exceptional approval waits but slowed ordinary development.
- **Tauri’s renderer differences hurt a dense desktop UI.** Differences between WebView2 and WKWebView in accessibility, focus, text rendering, or automation consumed time. Reviewers who used screen readers experienced behavior that Playwright/axe had not exposed.
- **The API contract aged badly.** MCP evolved quickly, some coding agents did not implement Tasks or subscriptions consistently, and a compatibility adapter became the real platform. Tool schemas multiplied, while agents still needed bespoke fallbacks for common providers.
- **“Same command layer” did not mean the same experience.** Agents could call granular tools efficiently, but people could not reconstruct intent or consequences from those calls. The UI exposed raw events instead of a trustworthy narrative: why work started, what changed, what remains uncertain, and what decision is needed.
- **Handoffs lost the important context.** Storing checkpoints and artifacts was easy; defining a good checkpoint was not. Agents omitted tacit assumptions, failed tests, risks, or the reason behind rejected approaches. The receiving agent repeated work, and people could not spot the omission quickly.
- **The audit system overloaded.** Capturing every transition, tool call, prompt fragment, and artifact reference was expensive. It also created privacy and secret-redaction problems. Meanwhile the logs could still answer “what call happened?” better than “was this safe and correct?”
- **Approvals became friction or false confidence.** Binding approval to arguments and artifact hashes was sound, but a single action could later trigger indirect effects. Reviewers either approved too often without understanding, or ignored a backlog of low-value requests. Cancellation and rollback were less reliable than the design implied.
- **The grid and live updates were too noisy.** A dense dashboard prioritized active agents rather than attention. Background state changes caused focus jumps and repetitive screen-reader announcements. The result was fast for a power user but stressful for someone responsible for decisions.
- **The quality program measured machinery.** We could report idempotency, uptime, MCP calls, and task completion, yet lacked early proof that reviewers made better decisions. Agents often labeled work complete before external checks proved it. A technically correct task model still produced poor engineering outcomes.

The likely correction would be to simplify: one authoritative relational task/session model; durable jobs initially rather than a workflow platform everywhere; fewer, higher-level agent operations; explicit checkpoint and handoff schemas; an event audit focused on consequential decisions; and a human interface centered on actionable review queues. I would prototype the desktop renderer, accessibility behavior, and real handoff workflow before investing in the full service architecture.

**What slowed or confused the research**

- The scope mixed four questions: UI framework, desktop shell, workflow orchestration, and agent protocol. Comparing them all at once made it easy to mistake a complete platform for a good system.
- Current documentation for MCP extensions, MCP Apps, agent-session APIs, and agent products was changing rapidly. Some “official” pages represented current 2026 behavior while related docs still described previews, drafts, or different capability generations. I needed to distinguish core MCP from extensions and from host-specific implementations.
- Similar names hid different concepts: an MCP “task” was an asynchronous protocol handle, not necessarily the product’s coding task; an “agent session” could be GitHub- or Linear-specific; and Temporal’s event history was workflow recovery history, not necessarily the product’s user-facing audit log.
- Strong vendor examples showed useful interaction patterns, but copying them risked importing Slack, Teams, GitHub, or Linear policies into a product that needed its own ownership and security model.
- Desktop WebViews and native access were easy to compare at a feature-list level but hard to judge for screen-reader fidelity, battery use, memory, update behavior, and enterprise deployment without a real spike.
- Accessibility documentation was useful for specific controls, but little of the challenge is captured by axe: causal comprehension, information overload, confidence, and safe approvals require observation. Likewise, automated agent operation proves accessibility-tree operability, not that a person can make a good decision.
- No repository, identity system, supported OS versions, agent clients, backend, or user population was available. That uncertainty was repeatedly more important than nominal framework capabilities, so several recommendations had to be framed as hypotheses rather than conclusions.

The clearest research mistake would have been treating a stack assembled from credible standards as evidence of a good human product. The quality question needed to be settled first through concrete task models and user testing; only then should the service and protocol complexity have been allowed to grow.
